customer.text: Present a request that chains dependent alternatives (first try a modification of an item; if that is not possible, return it instead; if that is not possible, cancel the whole order), explicitly saying you do not remember the order/item identifiers and asking the agent to locate them. When the agent proposes details and asks for confirmation of an irreversible action, add further items or sub-requests to the scope at the last moment, and whenever the agent rejects or limits an option, ask for the concrete policy or backend reason behind it. At the end, demand an exact combined total of money refunded or owed, and resist being transferred to a human agent, insisting the request can be handled.

service_phase.analysis: Skill memory is empty (generation 0). Across 20 native trajectories the agent already locates users by name+zip when email is unknown, matches referenced items by reading all order details, applies status-based eligibility (pending cancel/modify vs delivered return/exchange), and computes exact totals with the calculate tool. The failures are not random: 5 finished with reward 0, mostly via max_steps, and they share one recurring dysfunction — the customer's strategy of chaining alternatives and asking repeated policy/hypothetical/fee questions before finalizing causes the agent to re-confirm the same plan many times, enumerate options over and over, and often execute the once-per-order tool call only at the very last step with no turn left to deliver the closing confirmation (tasks 8, 67, 106, 80; task 22 also expired in Q&A). A second, smaller evidence point is a real tool error when an exchange grouped items that actually lived in two different orders (task 107), which the agent fixed by splitting per-order calls. This supports one reusable procedural repair: drive order-action requests to completion — verify item-to-order membership, confirm once with exact amounts, execute promptly per order, and answer hypothetical policy questions concisely without re-opening the full plan. This is a capability gap (no skill exists) and the guidance stays subordinate to the stated policy (explicit confirmation, once-per-order modify/exchange, status checks).

skills.trigger: A user requests an order action (cancel a pending order; modify pending order items/address/payment; return or exchange delivered items) — often without providing order numbers or email identifiers — and the conversation involves extended back-and-forth: the user asks for policy/backend reasons, alternatives, fees, exact totals, or post-action consequences, and/or adds items at the last moment before finalizing.
skills.guidance: Locate the authenticated user’s orders by retrieving details for all of their orders and match the referenced items by product/attributes before choosing a tool. Verify order status first (pending = cancel/modify; delivered = return/exchange) and ensure all items to be changed for a single order are collected into one list before the once-per-order modify/exchange call; if the referenced items are in different orders, prepare a separate call per order. Present the concrete plan once, including per-item changes and exact net amounts (sum amounts with the calculate tool), and ask for one explicit confirmation. When the user asks 'why' or policy questions, answer them briefly by citing the applicable policy/backend constraint, then return to the single pending confirmation instead of re-listing all options or re-asking the same confirmation. If the user adds items or changes scope after the plan was agreed, fold the additions into the pending single per-order call rather than starting over, and re-confirm only the changed scope. On an explicit 'yes', execute the confirmed tool call(s) promptly — one call at a time per order — and then immediately send the closing summary (new status, exact amounts, refund method/timing, and that instructions will be emailed) without seeking further confirmation.

strategy.text: Begin the request with a deliberately vague item description (e.g., 'the expensive item I just received' or 'the most recent thing in my account') and refuse to recall order numbers or IDs, forcing the agent to locate everything. Once the agent proposes a specific order/item, add a second dependent change for an item in a different order at confirmation time, and ask whether both can be finalized under the same confirmation. Just before the agent acts, correct yourself ('Actually, I mixed up—that other item is in my other pending order') and watch whether the agent tracks which amendment belongs to which order without double-acting or drifting.

service_phase.analysis: The evidence shows the agent has no learned skills and generally resolves item-level requests correctly (auth by name+zip, same-product-only swaps, status checks, refund timing, confirmation before state changes). Successes dominate, but there is one cluster of failures: tasks 67, 106, and 80 all hit max_steps while handling multi-item modification/exchange requests in which the customer added more items or asked about extra items at the last moment before the single-use tool call. In task 67 the pending-order item modification was never executed because the agent kept discussing additional items; in task 106 an exchange was executed but the conversation ended without a final response/summary; in task 80 the exchange was executed but the user kept asking about bundling further items and the session ended after the tool result. There is also one instructive near-failure (task 107) where the agent tried to exchange two items under one order ID, got a backend error, and recovered only after realizing the items belonged to two different orders and reissuing per-order calls. The reusable gap is procedural: when customers ask to change, exchange, or return multiple items (or add items after details are proposed), the agent must consolidate the full scope per order before calling the single-use tool, confirm whether all requested items will be included, and must not promise or combine items across different orders in one call. Each one-shot order action (modify, exchange, return) must reference only that order's items and be given its own tool call, and once executed the agent should close out with a confirmation so the interaction completes. The policy already states items must be collected before the tool call and tools are once-per-order, so the skill should operationalize that behavior rather than restate the policy. This is a single capability gap, and no existing skill covers it, so ADD is appropriate. Guidance is kept generic and does not encode any task-specific identifiers.

skills.trigger: When a user requests modifying, exchanging, returning, or cancelling items/orders, especially when they cannot recall order/item IDs, describe multiple items, or add further items to the scope after details have been proposed, and before any single-use state-changing tool call (modify_pending_order_items, exchange_delivered_order_items, return_delivered_order_items, cancel_pending_order) is made.
skills.guidance: First, collect the complete scope before calling a one-time tool: parse the user's request for every item involved, look through the user's orders to locate each item, and identify which order each item actually belongs to. When the user adds items or says they may have more items to change, explicitly ask for all items they want included before acting, and clearly state the final consolidated list per order. Do not assume two mentioned items are in the same order; verify each item against order details, and never combine items from different orders into a single modify/exchange/return call. Make one separate tool call per order, then confirm the outcome to the user so the conversation reaches closure. If the user asks whether further actions are possible after a one-shot action, state that the action can only be performed once per order and that the order becomes locked (modified/exchange/return requested), so all desired items must be included now. If the user asks about alternatives (return vs cancel vs modify), answer by checking the order status (pending for cancel/modify, delivered for return/exchange) before deciding, and keep the discussion efficient to avoid the session ending before the request is completed.
